title: Vda. de Mapa v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. L-38972, September 28, 1987

properties.name: Residue of Concepcion Mapa de Hidrosollo's estate
properties.description: The decision describes the residue of the testatrix's parafernal and conjugal properties but does not state a monetary valuation.

properties.name: Ilaud lot in Dumarao
properties.description: The will allowed Salvador Genova to reside on this lot without rent during his lifetime.

persons.name: Salvador Genova
persons.role: Lifetime beneficiary of palay and free residence

dispositions.description: Ludovico was instituted universal heir to the residue, subject to the testamentary trust and charges, but his compulsory one-half legitime could not be burdened.
Ignacio represents the named group of thirteen nephews and nieces who were to enjoy the residue after Ludovico's death through the express trust; all thirteen are listed as persons in this record.
Lifetime delivery of twelve cavans of palay per year and rent-free residence on the Ilaud lot.

conditions.text: After Ludovico's death, the residue was to be enjoyed in common by the thirteen named nephews and nieces, without sale or encumbrance, under the joint administration of Ignacio Salazar and Luis Hidrosollo.

The beneficiaries were to give Salvador Genova twelve cavans of palay annually while he lived, conditioned on his helping Luis Hidrosollo collect harvests, and permit him to live rent-free on the Ilaud lot.

story.narrative: Concepcion Mapa de Hidrosollo executed a will on June 2, 1951. She instituted her husband, Ludovico Hidrosollo, as universal heir to the residue of her estate, but directed that after his death the residue be held and enjoyed in common by thirteen named nephews and nieces. The will imposed continuing duties in favor of Salvador Genova and restricted alienation and encumbrance. The dispute was whether the arrangement created an enforceable express trust and how far it could burden the surviving spouse's legitime.
story.circumstances: The Court treated the testamentary language and surrounding provisions as creating an express trust. Because Ludovico was a compulsory heir, the trust could operate only against the free half of the estate, not against his one-half legitime.
keyFacts: Thirteen nephews and nieces were specifically named as common beneficiaries after Ludovico's death.
Ignacio Salazar and Luis Hidrosollo were designated to administer the property jointly.
The beneficiaries were prohibited from selling or encumbering the property and were charged with supporting Salvador Genova in the manner stated in the will.

caseDetails.officialTitle: Corazon Mapa Vda. de Mapa v. Court of Appeals
caseDetails.nature: Petition concerning the interpretation and enforcement of a testamentary trust
proceduralHistory: The trial court and Court of Appeals construed the testamentary provisions concerning the residue and the beneficiaries' obligations.
The Supreme Court reviewed whether the will created a trust and the extent to which it could affect the surviving spouse's compulsory share.
issues: Whether the will created an express trust over the residue for the thirteen nephews and nieces.
Whether the trust and its restrictions could validly burden the surviving spouse's legitime.
rulings: The testamentary provisions created an express trust, considering the will as a whole and the duties imposed on the beneficiaries and administrators.
The trust was effective only over the free half because Ludovico's one-half legitime as surviving spouse could not be subject to a condition, burden, or substitution.
doctrines: No technical words are required to create an express trust when the testator's intent is clear from the will taken as a whole.
A compulsory heir's legitime cannot be impaired by testamentary conditions or charges; the disposition may operate only on the free portion.
provisions: Civil Code provisions on legitimes and testamentary trusts
recordLimitations: The published decision does not give estate valuations or a complete genealogical chart. Zero values mark facts not supplied by the record, not valueless property.
citationCorrections: The official docket is G.R. No. L-38972, not G.R. No. L-43872 as stated in the request.

explanation: This record visualizes the testamentary trust, the surviving spouse's protected share, and the duties attached to the residue. It does not assign invented monetary values.

properties.name: One-sixth interest in Escolta land and building
properties.description: Inventory value stated in the decision.

properties.description: Inventory value stated in the decision.

properties.name: 491 shares, Central Azucarera de la Carlota

generalLiabilities.label: Bank of the Philippine Islands debt

dispositions.description: The Court protected the widow's one-half legitime in full ownership.
One-half of the naked ownership of the disposable half, with reciprocal vulgar substitution between the grandnephews.
One-half of the naked ownership of the disposable half, with reciprocal vulgar substitution between the grandnephews.
Usufruct of the free half, with a simple substitution upon Wanda's death in favor of Juan Pablo Jankowski and Horace V. Ramirez in equal shares.

conditions.text: Wanda's usufruct was over the disposable half only; the attempted successive arrangement could not impair the widow's legitime, and only the valid simple substitution was preserved.

story.narrative: Jose Eugenio Ramirez, a Filipino, died in Spain on December 11, 1964. His only compulsory heir was his French wife, Marcelle Demoron de Ramirez. His will divided naked ownership and usufruct among his widow, two grandnephews, his companion Wanda de Wrobleski, and substitute usufructuaries. The controversy concerned the widow's legitime, the validity of successive substitutions, and whether an alien could receive a testamentary usufruct.
story.circumstances: The estate inventory stated gross assets of PHP 512,976.97, a PHP 5,000 debt, and net assets of PHP 507,976.97. The probate court admitted the will on July 27, 1965.
keyFacts: Marcelle was the only compulsory heir and was entitled to one-half of the estate in full ownership.
Roberto and Jorge received the naked ownership of the disposable half, subject to the valid usufruct.
Wanda's alien nationality did not bar a usufruct because a usufruct does not transfer title to land.

caseDetails.officialTitle: Testate Estate of Jose Eugenio Ramirez; Maria Luisa Palacios v. Marcelle D. Vda. de Ramirez, et al.
caseDetails.nature: Appeal in testate proceedings involving legitime, usufruct, and substitutions
proceduralHistory: The will was admitted to probate on July 27, 1965.
The lower court approved a project of partition, and objections concerning the widow's share, Wanda's usufruct, and the substitutions reached the Supreme Court.
issues: How the surviving widow's one-half legitime should be protected.
Whether the substitutions attached to the usufruct were valid.
Whether Wanda, an Austrian national, could validly receive a usufruct over Philippine property.
rulings: Marcelle was entitled to one-half of the estate in full ownership as her legitime.
The fideicommissary aspect was ineffective, but the valid simple substitutions were respected within the free portion.
Wanda could receive the usufruct because it did not vest title to land in her.
doctrines: Testamentary provisions are reduced or disregarded to the extent necessary to preserve a compulsory heir's legitime.
A prohibited or ineffective successive substitution may be severed while valid dispositions and simple substitutions are preserved.
The constitutional restriction on alien landholding does not prohibit an alien from receiving a usufruct that does not transfer title.
provisions: 1935 Constitution restriction on alien acquisition of private land
recordLimitations: The record supports the inventory figures and dispositive shares, but not current market values. The JSONL preserves historical amounts exactly as reported.

explanation: The estate card reproduces the reported historical inventory. Overlapping naked ownership and usufruct are described textually rather than summed as separate cash distributions.

title: Crisologo v. Singson, G.R. No. L-13876, February 28, 1962

properties.name: One-half of the house and 193-square-meter lot on Plaridel Street, Vigan
properties.description: Tax Declaration No. 10765-C; the decision does not state a monetary value.

persons.name: Evaristo Singson
persons.role: Substitute beneficiary named in the codicil

persons.name: Dionisio Singson
persons.role: Substitute beneficiary named in the codicil

dispositions.description: The codicil gave Consolacion one-half of the house and lot; if she died before or after the testatrix, the property was to pass to Evaristo, Manuel, and Dionisio or their forced heirs.

story.narrative: Leona Singson died single on January 13, 1948. By will and codicil she gave her grandniece, Consolacion Florentino de Crisologo, one-half of a house and residential lot in Vigan. The clause added that if Consolacion died before or after Leona, the property would pass to Evaristo, Manuel, and Dionisio Singson or their forced heirs. When Consolacion sought partition, the parties disputed whether the clause imposed a fideicommissary duty to preserve and transmit the property.
story.circumstances: The property was a 193-square-meter residential lot with a house on Plaridel Street, covered by Tax Declaration No. 10765-C.
keyFacts: The codicil did not expressly require Consolacion to preserve and transmit the property.
The named event was Consolacion's death, whether before or after Leona's death.
Consolacion and her husband sought partition of the co-owned property.

caseDetails.officialTitle: Consolacion Florentino de Crisologo, et al. v. Dr. Manuel Singson
caseDetails.nature: Action for partition requiring construction of a testamentary substitution
proceduralHistory: Consolacion and her husband brought an action to partition the Vigan house and lot.
The lower court treated the clause as a fideicommissary substitution and dismissed the complaint; the Supreme Court reviewed that construction.
issues: Whether the codicil created a fideicommissary substitution that required Consolacion to preserve and transmit the property, or only a simple substitution.
rulings: The clause created a simple or vulgar substitution, not a fideicommissary substitution.
Consolacion acquired ownership of the devised half and could demand partition.
doctrines: A fideicommissary substitution must be express and must impose a clear obligation on the first heir to preserve and transmit the property to the second heir.
A provision substituting another beneficiary if the first dies before or after the testator, without an express preservation duty, is construed as simple substitution.
recordLimitations: The decision identifies the property and its area but gives no valuation. The zero value is an unknown-value marker.

explanation: The relationship map emphasizes substitution rather than descent because the legal issue was the nature of the testamentary clause.

title: Rodriguez v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. L-28734, March 28, 1969

properties.name: Properties placed under Margarita Rodriguez's testamentary administration
properties.description: The reported decision discusses a trust-like administration and income scheme but does not provide a consolidated valuation in the cited record.

persons.name: Named testamentary beneficiaries
persons.role: Recipients of income and benefits under the will

dispositions.description: The will directed continued administration and payment of income to named beneficiaries, subject to a perpetual prohibition against alienation or mortgage.

conditions.text: Clause 10 prohibited alienation or mortgage of the affected properties forever. The Court sustained the restriction only for the twenty-year period permitted by law and treated the excess as void.

story.narrative: Margarita Rodriguez died in Manila on July 19, 1960 without compulsory heirs. Her will, later admitted to probate, arranged for the continued administration of property and the distribution of income to named beneficiaries. A clause prohibited alienation or mortgage forever. The dispute was whether the excessive restriction invalidated the testamentary plan or merely failed beyond the statutory limit.
story.circumstances: The will was admitted to probate on September 23, 1960, and a project of partition was approved on August 27, 1962.
keyFacts: Margarita had no compulsory heirs, so she could dispose of her estate subject to statutory limitations.
Clause 10 attempted to make the prohibition against alienation or mortgage perpetual.
The Court preserved the testamentary plan while limiting the restriction to twenty years.

caseDetails.nature: Review of a testamentary prohibition against alienation and the effect of partial invalidity
proceduralHistory: Margarita's will was admitted to probate and a project of partition was approved.
Litigation followed over whether the perpetual restriction defeated the dispositions or should be limited under Article 870.
issues: Whether a testamentary prohibition against alienation or mortgage in perpetuity invalidated the will's dispositions.
Whether the estate should pass by intestacy because part of the prohibition exceeded the statutory period.
rulings: The prohibition was effective only for twenty years and void beyond that period.
The excessive portion did not cause intestacy; the testatrix's lawful dispositions and principal testamentary intent were preserved.
doctrines: A disposition prohibiting alienation for more than twenty years is void only as to the excess unless the invalid part is inseparable from the testamentary plan.
Courts should uphold the testator's intent so far as legally possible rather than create intestacy unnecessarily.
provisions: Civil Code rules favoring testacy and severability of invalid conditions
recordLimitations: The public decision identifies the testamentary scheme and dates but does not provide enough data for an estate computation or a complete beneficiary-by-beneficiary graph.
citationCorrections: The official decision date is March 28, 1969, not March 16, 1969 as stated in the request.

explanation: This scenario focuses on the twenty-year limit on prohibitions to alienate. No estate value is inferred.

title: Rabadilla v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 113725, June 29, 2000

properties.name: 511,855-square-meter portion of Lot 1392, Bacolod Cadastre
properties.description: Covered by TCT No. RT-4002; no monetary valuation is stated in the decision.

dispositions.description: Aleja's codicil devised the lot to Jorge, with his spouse and children to inherit if he predeceased her and with the annual sugar obligation binding successors and transferees.
Lifetime annual delivery of seventy-five piculs of export sugar and twenty-five piculs of domestic sugar.

conditions.text: The landholder must deliver annually to Maria Marlena, while she lives, seventy-five piculs of export sugar and twenty-five piculs of domestic sugar. Any buyer, lessee, or mortgagee must assume the charge; nonperformance authorizes seizure and reversion for the benefit of Aleja's near descendants.

story.narrative: Aleja Belleza's codicil devised a large portion of Lot 1392 in Bacolod to Dr. Jorge Rabadilla. The devise carried a lifetime obligation to deliver one hundred piculs of sugar annually to Maria Marlena Coscolluela Belleza and required every transferee to assume the same duty. Jorge later died, and his wife and children succeeded to the property. After repeated noncompliance, Maria Marlena sought reconveyance under the sanction written into the codicil.
story.circumstances: Jorge died in 1983. His heirs mortgaged the property to Philippine National Bank and Republic Planters Bank and failed to make the annual deliveries beginning in 1985. A PHP 105,000 settlement was only partially performed, including a delivery of 50.80 piculs for crop year 1988-1989.
keyFacts: The devise expressly bound Jorge's heirs and any buyer, lessee, or mortgagee.
Failure to deliver the stipulated sugar triggered a right to seize the property and return it to Aleja's estate for her near descendants.
The Court classified the institution as modal, not as a simple or fideicommissary substitution.

caseDetails.nature: Petition concerning a modal testamentary institution and enforcement of an attached charge
proceduralHistory: Maria Marlena sued after the annual sugar deliveries were not made.
The Court of Appeals ordered reconveyance; the Supreme Court reviewed the nature and transmissibility of the obligation.
issues: Whether the sugar obligation was merely personal to Jorge or passed to his heirs and transferees.
Whether the codicil created a modal institution, a substitution, or an unenforceable perpetual burden.
Whether noncompliance justified reconveyance under the codicil.
rulings: The obligation attached to the devise and passed to Jorge's heirs under the codicil and the law on transmission of hereditary rights and obligations.
The disposition was a modal institution under Article 882, not a simple or fideicommissary substitution.
The stipulated consequence of nonperformance was enforceable, and reconveyance to Aleja's estate was affirmed.
doctrines: In a modal institution, the instituted heir receives the property but must comply with the charge or application imposed by the testator.
Hereditary rights and obligations that are not purely personal pass to heirs from the moment of death.
A compromise by successors cannot defeat a testamentary charge and sanction in favor of a beneficiary who invokes the will.
provisions: Civil Code provisions on testamentary conditions and modes
recordLimitations: The decision supplies land area and performance quantities but no estate valuation. Sugar quantities are obligations, not estate cash values.

explanation: The estate view links the devise and legacy to the same land because the annual sugar charge follows the property and its successors.

title: Rosales v. Rosales, G.R. No. L-40789, February 27, 1987, 148 SCRA 69

properties.name: Intestate estate of Petra Rosales
properties.description: The decision states a gross value of approximately PHP 30,000 but does not state liabilities or a reliable net estate.

persons.name: Irenea Rosales
persons.role: Widow of Carterio; claimant but not Petra's intestate heir

story.narrative: Petra Rosales died intestate in Cebu on February 26, 1971. She was survived by her husband Fortunato, two living children, and a grandson whose father Carterio had predeceased Petra. Carterio's widow, Irenea, claimed a share in Petra's estate. The case asked whether a daughter-in-law could inherit from her mother-in-law by intestate succession or representation.
story.circumstances: The gross estate was reported at approximately PHP 30,000. The trial court allotted one-fourth shares to Fortunato, Magna, Antonio, and Macikequerox; Irenea challenged her exclusion.
keyFacts: Carterio died before Petra and left his widow Irenea and child Macikequerox.
Macikequerox stood in Carterio's place by representation in the direct descending line.
Irenea was related to Petra only by affinity, not by blood, and was not included among Petra's intestate heirs.

caseDetails.nature: Appeal in intestate proceedings on representation and the rights of a daughter-in-law
proceduralHistory: The trial court approved a division among the surviving spouse, two living children, and the representing grandson.
Irenea appealed her exclusion from Petra's intestate estate.
issues: Whether a daughter-in-law is an intestate heir of her mother-in-law.
Whether Carterio's son could represent him in Petra's succession.
rulings: Irenea was not Petra's intestate heir because affinity did not place her within the classes called by law.
Macikequerox inherited by representation of his predeceased father in the direct descending line.
doctrines: Representation is a right created by law by which a representative is raised to the place and degree of the person represented.

In the direct line, representation takes place only in the descending line and operates through blood relationship; a surviving spouse does not represent a deceased spouse in the latter's parent's estate.
provisions: Civil Code rules on intestate succession of surviving spouses and legitimate descendants
recordLimitations: Only an approximate gross estate value is reported. Assets and liabilities are therefore left at zero to avoid presenting the gross estimate as a net distributable estate.

explanation: This is an intestate-succession case, so the absence of testamentary dispositions is a material fact rather than missing content.

title: Francisco v. Francisco-Alfonso, G.R. No. 138774, March 8, 2001, 354 SCRA 112

properties.name: Residential parcel in Lolomboy, Bocaue, Bulacan (TCT No. T-32740)
properties.description: One of the two parcels constituting Gregorio's only property; no adjudicated market value is stated.

properties.name: Residential parcel in Lolomboy, Bocaue, Bulacan (TCT No. T-117160)
properties.description: One of the two parcels constituting Gregorio's only property; no adjudicated market value is stated.

persons.name: Aida Francisco-Alfonso
persons.role: Sole legitimate child and compulsory heir

persons.name: Regina Francisco
persons.role: Acknowledged natural child and purported buyer

persons.name: Zenaida Pascual
persons.role: Julia's daughter by her lawful husband and purported buyer

story.narrative: Gregorio Francisco and his lawful wife Cirila de la Cruz had one legitimate daughter, Aida. Gregorio later lived with Julia Mendoza and had children outside the marriage, including Regina. On August 15, 1983, Gregorio purportedly sold his only two residential parcels in Bulacan to Regina and Zenaida Pascual for PHP 25,000. After Gregorio died on July 20, 1990, Aida challenged the conveyance as simulated and intended to defeat her legitime.
story.circumstances: The two parcels were Gregorio's only property. Zenaida was Julia's daughter by her lawful husband and was not Gregorio's blood descendant.
keyFacts: The alleged buyers failed to prove actual payment of the PHP 25,000 consideration.
Gregorio remained in possession and the circumstances supported simulation.
As Gregorio's sole legitimate child, Aida was entitled to one-half of his hereditary estate as legitime.

caseDetails.officialTitle: Regina Francisco and Zenaida Pascual v. Aida Francisco-Alfonso
caseDetails.nature: Action to annul a simulated sale that prejudiced a compulsory heir's legitime
proceduralHistory: Aida sued to annul the deed covering Gregorio's two parcels.
The lower courts found the sale simulated; the Supreme Court reviewed the evidence and the effect on Aida's hereditary rights.
issues: Whether the deed of sale was supported by consideration and represented a genuine conveyance.
Whether the transfer could be sustained despite its effect of depriving the sole legitimate child of her legitime.
rulings: The purported sale was absolutely simulated and void for lack of consideration.
Even apart from simulation, the transaction could not be used to defeat Aida's protected legitime; the parcels returned to Gregorio's estate.
doctrines: An absolutely simulated contract is void and produces no transfer of ownership.
A legitimate child is a compulsory heir entitled to one-half of the hereditary estate when the child is the sole legitimate descendant, absent a valid cause and form of disinheritance.
provisions: Civil Code rules on simulation, consideration, and disinheritance
recordLimitations: The PHP 25,000 figure is the recited sale price, not an adjudicated estate valuation. Property gross values remain unknown.

explanation: Because the challenged conveyance was inter vivos and void, it is shown in the case story rather than misclassified as a devise or legacy.

title: Baritua v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 82233, March 22, 1990, 183 SCRA 565

properties.name: Wrongful-death and property-damage claims arising from the November 7, 1979 collision
properties.description: The decision concerns who could receive or pursue the claim; it does not treat the tortfeasors as holders of the decedent's estate.

persons.name: Child of Bienvenido and Alicia Nacario
Nicolas Nacario
persons.role: Father of Bienvenido and excluded ascendant

persons.name: Victoria Ronda Nacario
persons.role: Mother of Bienvenido and excluded ascendant

story.narrative: Bienvenido Nacario died in a collision between a passenger bus and a tricycle on November 7, 1979. The bus operator, driver, and insurer later paid his widow Alicia PHP 18,500 in exchange for a release and affidavit of desistance. Bienvenido's parents subsequently sued for damages and reimbursement of alleged loans and funeral expenses. The succession question was whether the widow and child were the successors entitled to settle the claim and whether the parents could inherit concurrently.
story.circumstances: The payment and release were executed on March 27, 1980. The parents filed their own action on September 2, 1981.
keyFacts: Alicia and Bienvenido's child were his heirs and successors.
The presence of a legitimate child excluded the decedent's parents from intestate succession.
Estrangement between spouses is not a statutory disqualification from inheritance.
Claims for loans or funeral expenses are properly asserted against the estate, not converted into independent claims against the tortfeasors.

caseDetails.officialTitle: Jose Baritua and Edgar Bitancor v. Court of Appeals, Nicolas Nacario and Victoria Ronda Nacario
caseDetails.nature: Petition involving settlement of a death claim and priority among intestate heirs
proceduralHistory: The widow executed a release after receiving PHP 18,500 from the insurer and petitioners.
The decedent's parents later obtained relief in the lower courts; the Supreme Court reviewed their standing and the effect of the settlement.
issues: Whether payment to and release by the surviving spouse and child extinguished the claim arising from Bienvenido's death.
Whether the decedent's parents inherited concurrently with his legitimate child.
Whether estrangement disqualified the surviving spouse.
rulings: Payment to the widow and child, as Bienvenido's successors, extinguished the claim covered by the release.
The parents were excluded from intestate succession by the surviving legitimate child.
Mere estrangement did not disqualify Alicia as surviving spouse and heir.
doctrines: Legitimate parents and ascendants inherit only in default of legitimate children and descendants.
A surviving spouse is not disqualified from inheritance by mere factual separation or estrangement without a statutory ground.
Personal money claims against a decedent belong in estate proceedings.
provisions: Rules on claims against a decedent's estate
recordLimitations: This is not a testate-disposition case. The JSONL includes it because it directly addresses heir priority and succession to a cause of action.

explanation: No will or testamentary disposition existed. The scenario focuses on identifying the lawful successors to the death claim.

title: Van Dorn v. Romillo, Jr., G.R. No. L-68470, October 8, 1985, 139 SCRA 139

properties.name: Galleon Shop business and alleged conjugal assets
properties.description: Richard alleged that the business was conjugal; the Nevada divorce record stated that the parties had no community property or obligations.

persons.name: Theodore Van Dorn
persons.role: Alice's husband after the Nevada divorce

persons.name: First child of Alice and Richard
Second child of Alice and Richard

story.narrative: Filipino citizen Alice Reyes and American citizen Richard Upton married in Hong Kong in 1972 and later lived in the Philippines, where they had two children. They obtained a divorce in Nevada in 1982, and Alice later married Theodore Van Dorn. Richard then sued in the Philippines for an accounting of the Galleon Shop as alleged conjugal property. The Court considered the effect of the foreign divorce on Richard's claimed rights as spouse, including potential succession rights.
story.circumstances: The children were born on April 4, 1973 and December 18, 1975. Richard filed his Philippine action on June 8, 1983. The Nevada divorce record recited that the parties had no community property or obligations.
keyFacts: Richard was an American national whose personal status and capacity were governed by his national law.
The Nevada divorce was binding on Richard, who could not continue to assert marital rights in the Philippines after obtaining the divorce.
Treating him as still married would improperly preserve rights to alleged conjugal property and potential inheritance from Alice.

caseDetails.officialTitle: Alice Reyes Van Dorn v. Hon. Manuel V. Romillo, Jr. and Richard Upton
caseDetails.nature: Petition on the effect of a foreign divorce obtained by an alien spouse
proceduralHistory: Richard sued in the Regional Trial Court for an accounting of the Galleon Shop and alleged conjugal property.
Alice moved to dismiss based on the Nevada divorce; after the motion was denied, she sought relief in the Supreme Court.
issues: Whether the Nevada divorce bound the American former husband and prevented him from asserting marital property rights in the Philippines.
Whether he retained standing as Alice's husband after the divorce.
rulings: The divorce was binding on Richard under his national law, and he could no longer sue as Alice's husband.
Richard was estopped from claiming rights flowing from a marriage that his own divorce had dissolved.
doctrines: An alien spouse who validly obtains a foreign divorce is bound by it and cannot continue to assert marital rights against the Filipino former spouse in the Philippines.
After the foreign divorce, the alien is no longer entitled to rights in alleged conjugal property or to potential inheritance merely by claiming continuing spousal status.
provisions: Conflict-of-laws rules on status, capacity, and foreign divorce
recordLimitations: This is a marital-status case with succession implications, not an estate proceeding. No person in the case was the decedent whose estate was being distributed.

explanation: The relationship map shows historical and subsequent marriages, but the story and doctrine make clear that Richard's Nevada divorce ended his claimed spousal status.

title: Uson v. Del Rosario, et al., G.R. No. L-4963, January 29, 1953, 92 Phil. 530

properties.name: Five parcels of land in Labrador, Pangasinan
properties.description: Faustino Nebreda left five parcels; the decision does not state their monetary value.

properties.name: Parcel delivered to Maria Uson under the 1931 separation document
properties.description: The document treated the parcel as alimony and purported to waive future inheritance rights.

persons.name: Maria Uson
persons.role: Lawful surviving spouse and sole heir under the governing law

story.narrative: Maria Uson was the lawful wife of Faustino Nebreda. After they separated, Faustino lived with Maria del Rosario and had four illegitimate children. Faustino died in 1945 leaving five parcels of land in Labrador, Pangasinan. Maria Uson sued to recover the properties. The defendants relied on a 1931 separation document in which Maria received one parcel as alimony and purportedly renounced future inheritance, and they also invoked the later New Civil Code rights of illegitimate children.
story.circumstances: Faustino died before the New Civil Code took effect. The hereditary rights of his lawful widow vested at his death under the law then governing.
keyFacts: The 1931 document could not validly renounce an inheritance that had not yet opened.
The New Civil Code could not be applied retroactively to impair Maria Uson's vested rights.
An alleged oral donation of land at Faustino's wake was ineffective without the formalities required for a donation of immovable property.

caseDetails.officialTitle: Maria Uson v. Maria del Rosario, et al.
caseDetails.nature: Recovery of hereditary land involving vested succession rights, future inheritance, and retroactivity
proceduralHistory: Maria Uson sued Maria del Rosario and the four children to recover Faustino's five parcels.
The lower court ruled for Maria Uson, and the defendants appealed to the Supreme Court.
issues: Whether the 1931 separation document validly waived Maria Uson's future inheritance.
Whether the New Civil Code could retroactively grant hereditary rights to the illegitimate children at the expense of rights vested in 1945.
Whether an alleged oral donation of land was valid.
rulings: The purported waiver of future inheritance was ineffective because succession had not yet opened.
Maria Uson's rights vested at Faustino's death under the old Civil Code and could not be impaired by retroactive application of the New Civil Code.
The alleged donation of real property was invalid for failure to comply with the required public-document and acceptance formalities.
doctrines: Hereditary rights are transmitted from the moment of the decedent's death and are governed by the law then in force.
A contract or renunciation concerning future inheritance is void except in cases expressly authorized by law.
New legislation cannot be applied retroactively to prejudice vested hereditary rights.
provisions: Civil Code formalities for donation of immovable property
recordLimitations: The decision identifies five parcels but does not provide land areas, titles, or valuations sufficient for computation.
citationCorrections: The official docket is G.R. No. L-4963, not G.R. No. L-4693 as stated in the request.

explanation: This is an intestate case. The absence of dispositions is deliberate; the controlling questions were when hereditary rights vested and whether they had been validly waived.

source.title: Uson v. Del Rosario, et al.
